clinicalPearls: A rare autosomal recessive purine-salvage enzyme defect causing a T-cell-predominant combined immunodeficiency, distinct from adenosine deaminase deficiency.
The combination of progressive cellular immunodeficiency with prominent neurological impairment is the clinical signature that should prompt testing.
Neurological features (developmental delay, spasticity, ataxia, movement disorder) affect the majority and may precede overt infections.
Autoimmune phenomena, particularly autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and cytopenias, are characteristically associated.
A markedly low serum uric acid (hypouricaemia) is a valuable and inexpensive biochemical clue reflecting the blocked purine pathway.
T-cell numbers and function decline progressively, while B cells and immunoglobulins are relatively preserved early, unlike classical severe combined immunodeficiency.
Accumulated deoxyguanosine triphosphate is toxic to developing thymocytes and underlies the selective T-cell depletion.
Haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation can correct the immunodeficiency but does not reverse established neurological damage, so early diagnosis is critical.
reference.pathophysiology: Purine nucleoside phosphorylase deficiency results from biallelic loss-of-function mutations in the PNP gene, encoding an enzyme of the purine salvage pathway that catalyses the phosphorolysis of inosine, deoxyinosine, guanosine and deoxyguanosine. Its absence leads to accumulation of these substrates and, critically, to a build-up of deoxyguanosine that is phosphorylated within cells, especially by deoxycytidine kinase in immature T lymphocytes, to deoxyguanosine triphosphate. High intracellular deoxyGTP inhibits ribonucleotide reductase and is selectively toxic to developing thymocytes, producing a progressive, T-cell-predominant lymphopenia; because the salvage burden falls disproportionately on the T lineage, B cells and immunoglobulin production are comparatively spared in the early course, distinguishing the biochemical phenotype from adenosine deaminase deficiency. The blocked pathway also diverts less purine to the terminal step catalysed by xanthine oxidase, so urate generation falls and serum and urinary uric acid are characteristically low. Neurotoxicity, thought to reflect accumulation of guanosine-derived metabolites in the central nervous system, produces the prominent spasticity, developmental delay, ataxia and movement disorder, and immune dysregulation predisposes to autoimmune cytopenias; over time the combined immune deficit renders patients vulnerable to viral, fungal and opportunistic infection.
additionalDifferentials: Other forms of severe combined immunodeficiency
Combined immunodeficiency with predominant neurological disease
Cerebral palsy or inherited metabolic encephalopathy (for the neurology)
additionalInvestigations: Serum and urinary uric acid demonstrating characteristic hypouricaemia
PNP enzyme activity assay in erythrocytes
Lymphocyte subsets showing progressive T-cell lymphopenia with relatively preserved B cells
Serum immunoglobulins and specific antibody responses
Neuroimaging and developmental assessment for the neurological component
Direct antiglobulin test and blood film when autoimmune cytopenia is suspected
redFlags: Progressive neurological deterioration in an infant with recurrent infection
Opportunistic or disseminated viral or fungal infection indicating advancing T-cell failure
Autoimmune haemolytic anaemia or severe cytopenia
Administration of live vaccines or non-irradiated blood products in a child with combined immunodeficiency
Failure to thrive with lymphopenia and unexplained low uric acid
reference.prognosis: Untreated, the disorder is usually fatal in childhood from infection or neurological decline. Haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation can restore immune function, but neurological deficits present at transplant generally persist, so outcome hinges on early recognition and intervention.
pitfalls: Assuming all purine-salvage combined immunodeficiency is adenosine deaminase deficiency and not testing PNP
Attributing the neurological picture to cerebral palsy and overlooking the underlying immunodeficiency
Missing the diagnostic clue of a low uric acid on routine biochemistry
Transfusing non-irradiated cellular blood products, risking transfusion-associated graft-versus-host disease
Expecting transplantation to reverse established neurological damage and delaying referral
management: Pursue allogeneic haematopoietic stem-cell transplantation, the only intervention capable of correcting the progressive T-cell immunodeficiency
Provide antimicrobial prophylaxis covering Pneumocystis with co-trimoxazole plus antifungal and antiviral agents, and immunoglobulin replacement as humoral function fails
Transfuse only irradiated, cytomegalovirus-safe, leucodepleted blood products and withhold live vaccines
Manage the characteristic autoimmune haemolytic anaemia and cytopenias with corticosteroids and additional immunosuppression
Support the neurological component of developmental delay, spasticity and movement disorder with neurology input and physical, occupational and speech therapy
Monitor lymphocyte subsets, immunoglobulins and for opportunistic infection, and track immune reconstitution after transplantation
Arrange genetic counselling and testing of at-risk relatives for this autosomal recessive PNP defect
